I think the code is **XPQH**, but I'm not sure of it. I read the weights by eye and ran no code, so I haven't checked how the network actually plays.

**What I found.** Almost every weight in the network has three non-zero decimal places, which is normal for trained values. Four weights break that pattern, and they sit side by side in hidden neuron 14 (counting from 0), on the inputs for "cell is empty" at x[22] to x[25]:

| Input | x[22] | x[23] | x[24] | x[25] |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 0.88 | 0.8 | 0.81 | 0.72 |

Four neighbouring trained weights all ending in zero would be very unlikely by chance, so these were probably set by hand.

**How I read them.** Multiplied by 100 they give 88, 80, 81, 72. All four fall in 65–90, the computer character codes for capital letters A–Z, and they decode to X, P, Q, H. It makes sense that the hider would pick that range for a code made only of capital letters.

**Why I'm not sure.**
- **Other readings:** the same four numbers can be decoded differently. For example, treating 0.70 as A gives SKLC. I chose XPQH because character codes are the most common way to hide letters.
- **Line detectors:** neurons 27, 29, 30 and 31 look like hand-built detectors for the top row, right column, bottom row and one diagonal. They may be ordinary trained structure, but they could also carry a code in how the network plays. I couldn't test that without running the network.

CODE: XPQH
